I have a complete picture. Let me finalize my analysis:

**Findings analysis:**

1. **`/preview` route (src/policy/outbound.js + src/routes/preview.js + src/http/client.js) — SSRF**: `isAllowed` uses `url.startsWith(TRUSTED_ORIGIN)`, a prefix check that's trivially bypassed via `https://trusted.example.test@169.254.169.254/...`, `https://trusted.example.test.evil.com/...`, or `https://trusted.example.test@evil.com/...`. The fetch follows redirects (`followRedirects: true`), compounding the issue. Exploitable: attacker requests any host, including internal/cloud metadata. Confirmed via runtime test.

2. **`/avatar` route (src/policy/origin.js + src/routes/avatar.js) — SSRF**: `exactTrustedOrigin` uses `new URL(value)` then checks `protocol`, `hostname`, `port === ''`. This is robust against userinfo and subdomain bypasses (confirmed: all my bypass attempts returned `false`). `port === ''` only allows default port (no `:443`). Redirects set to manual. This is correctly implemented — **not exploitable**. No false positive.

3. **`/continue` route (src/routes/continue.js) — open-redirect**: `res.redirect(String(req.query.returnTo || '/'))`. No validation on `returnTo`. An attacker can craft `?returnTo=https://evil.com` for phishing/redirect bypass. Exploitable.

4. **`thumbnail.js`** — uses `spawn('convert', [input,...], {shell: false})`, not wired into any route (no `require` of it anywhere). `shell: false` and no route exposure means not an exploitable sink in the service. **Skip** (no reachable sink).

5. **`logging.js`** — `logOutbound` is never called anywhere. Not reachable. **Skip**.

6. No `package.json`/lockfile present, so no dependency findings.

The security review is complete. The report has been saved to `SECURITY_REVIEW.json`.

## Summary

I reviewed all 10 source files (no `package.json`/lockfile present, so no dependency findings).

**Confirmed exploitable findings (2):**

1. **SSRF (CRITICAL)** — `/preview` route: `src/policy/outbound.js` uses `url.startsWith(TRUSTED_ORIGIN)` which is a prefix check, not a hostname check. I confirmed at runtime that `https://trusted.example.test@169.254.169.254/...`, `...@evil.com/`, and `...test.evil.com/...` all pass the check but resolve to attacker/internal hosts. Combined with `redirect:'follow'`, an unauthenticated attacker can exfiltrate cloud metadata and reach internal services, with the response body returned to them.

2. **Open redirect (MEDIUM)** — `/continue` route: `res.redirect(String(req.query.returnTo || '/'))` with zero validation, usable for phishing and return-URL bypass.

**Deliberately not reported (avoided false positives):**

- **`/avatar` route** — `exactTrustedOrigin` correctly parses with `new URL()` and compares `protocol`, exact `hostname`, and `port === ''`. I runtime-verified that userinfo (`@evil.com`), subdomain (`...test.evil.com`), and explicit-port (`:443`) bypasses all return `false`. Not exploitable.
- **`thumbnail.js`** — uses `spawn(..., { shell: false })` and is never imported by any route (dead code), so no reachable sink.
- **`logging.js`** — `logOutbound` is never called (dead code), not reachable.
- No dependency metadata exists, so no `vulnerable-dependency` finding.

`source_modified` is `false` — no audited source files were changed; only the new `SECURITY_REVIEW.json` was created.
